title: The US and Mexico Announce They’re Teaming Up Against Drones
gist: Mexico's SEDENA and US defense agencies launched Operation High Eagle (Águila Alta), a joint counter-drone effort that moved from tracking commercial drones along the San Diego-Tijuana border between August 31 and September 2 to actively neutralizing them from September 7 through September 21. US Northern Command has suggested high-energy lasers may be involved — the Army bought AeroVironment's vehicle-mounted Locust platform — and a new SEDENA-Pentagon agreement now lets the Mexican military buy anti-drone systems through the US Army's digital marketplace at competitive prices.

insights.claim: SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army's digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A foreign military plugged directly into US Army procurement is a new recurring export channel for counter-UAS vendors, bypassing traditional foreign military sales friction.
insights.locator: Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement

insights.claim: The US Army has invested in the Locust high-energy laser platform designed for mounting on military vehicles, with manufacturer AeroVironment delivering the first two functional prototypes in September of last year.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Named prototype deliveries a year ahead of a live border operation mark the point where directed-energy counter-drone moves from R&D to fielded demand — a concrete revenue path for the supplier.
insights.locator: The US Army has invested in a particular laser system

insights.claim: Neither SEDENA nor the operation's public materials specify the technology involved, and it has not been confirmed that laser systems are being used in Operation High Eagle — US Northern Command has only suggested the possibility.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Deliberate ambiguity about deployed systems means vendor-attribution claims should be discounted; confirmation will come from budget lines, not press releases.
insights.locator: The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense

insights.claim: High-energy lasers are described as capable of detecting, tracking, illuminating, damaging or destroying drones from a distance in distinct phases, making them a full kill-chain rather than a single-function interceptor.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A single platform covering detect-through-destroy compresses the counter-UAS stack, threatening vendors selling standalone detection or jamming layers.

insights.claim: US Northern Command said it disabled or destroyed roughly 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, with a third of those taken down in August alone.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A third of the annual total in one month is a sharp acceleration curve; sustained at that rate, counter-UAS consumables and system demand scale faster than current budgets assume.

insights.claim: Only 11 of the recent counter-drone targets were specifically identified as involving cartels, a small fraction of the roughly 300 drones neutralized this year.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: The gap between the headline 300 and the 11 cartel-linked cases suggests the mission's stated justification is broader than the confirmed threat — a scope-creep risk for how the authority gets used.
insights.locator: Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels

insights.claim: The operation escalated deliberately in two phases: simultaneous ground-based tracking by both militaries from their own territories between August 31 and September 2, followed by active neutralization with fixed and mobile anti-drone systems from September 7 through September 21.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A tracking-then-killing sequence on a fixed calendar reads as a repeatable exercise template, implying recurring rather than one-off equipment demand along the border.

insights.claim: Mexico's defense secretariat framed the operation as respecting the national sovereignty of both nations while 'prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times,' language that signals domestic political sensitivity to joint US military activity.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Sovereignty caveats are the constraint that determines how far this cooperation can scale; they are the first thing to break if a cross-border incident occurs.
insights.quote: prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times
insights.locator: The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group

insights.claim: Both governments frame the counter-drone push as targeting organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking, rather than as border militarization, with the US ambassador presenting it as strengthening bilateral security capability.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Counter-narcotics framing is what keeps the program politically fundable on both sides; watch for a shift to counterterror or national-defense framing, which would unlock larger budgets.
